title: Capstone: Image Models
blurb: Tests reusing one backbone for transfer, conditioning and evaluation, few-shot feature extraction against fine-tuning, the BatchNorm eval-mode bug, posterior collapse in a conditional VAE, and why classifier accuracy alone can't certify a generator.

refLinks.label: §75.2.1 Chaining Real Pieces Together Surfaces What Isolated Demos Cannot
§75.2.2 The Conditioning Signal Is the Backbone’s Own Embedding, Not a Fresh Label
§75.2.3 A Frozen Backbone Must Actually Be Frozen
§75.2.4 Classification Correctness and Distributional Realism Are Different Things

questions.prompt: Why does the capstone reuse one backbone for conditioning and evaluation, instead of separate demos?
options: Separate demos can't run on the same dataset.
The backbone is the only model that can read 8×8 images.
Bugs at the seams only show up when pieces connect.
It saves training time, which is the main goal of a capstone.
questions.explanation: The pipeline's two seams surfaced a real evaluation bug and a real hyperparameter failure that no single chapter would have caught.

refLinks.label: §75.2.1 Chaining Real Pieces Together Surfaces What Isolated Demos Cannot

questions.prompt: With 8 labelled examples per new class, which transfer approach won?
options: They tied within noise
Training from scratch, which beat both
Fine-tuning, at 95.6%
Feature extraction, at 95.6% against 87.9% for fine-tuning
questions.explanation: Unfreezing the residual block at a small learning rate generalised better here, even with 16 labelled examples in all.

questions.prompt: Why was the backbone's learning rate (1e-4) kept far below the new head's (1e-2)?
options: To make the head train more slowly than the backbone
To avoid catastrophic forgetting of the pretrained classes
To reduce the number of training epochs needed
Because BatchNorm can't handle large learning rates
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning isn't free. Aggressive updates can wipe out what the backbone learned on the original 8 classes.

questions.prompt: What does conditioning on the backbone's per-class mean embedding imply for unseen classes 8 and 9?
options: They can't be generated at all.
Their conditioning is perfect, since embeddings are always well separated.
Their conditioning is less distinct.
Their embeddings are identical to classes 0 and 1.
questions.explanation: Their embeddings were 1.35 apart, against 2.6–7.6 for most pretrained pairs. The signal inherits what the backbone learned.

refLinks.label: §75.2.2 The Conditioning Signal Is the Backbone’s Own Embedding, Not a Fresh Label

questions.prompt: Before calling .eval(), class-conditional accuracy was exactly chance, 8 of 80. What caused it?
options: BatchNorm used each batch's own statistics.
The test labels were shuffled by mistake.
The backbone's weights were reset during generation.
The generator had collapsed to a single image.
questions.explanation: In training mode, BatchNorm uses per-batch statistics. Similar generated images made those statistics amplify noise and corrupt every embedding.

questions.prompt: When does Procedure 75.2 say to call .eval()?
options: Only at final deployment, after all evaluation
Never, since torch.no_grad() covers the same thing
Right after training, before any reuse
Before every training step, to stabilise gradients
questions.explanation: no_grad stops gradients but doesn't switch BatchNorm to running statistics. The two are separate disciplines.

questions.prompt: The conditional VAE at β = 0.5 had a KL loss near zero and outputs that ignored the condition. What fixed it?
options: Doubling the latent dimension
Raising β to 1.0
Calling .eval() on the VAE
Lowering β to 0.1
questions.explanation: That's posterior collapse from β too high. At 0.1 the KL settled at a healthy 0.0197.

questions.prompt: Why does Procedure 75.3 say to watch the KL term separately from the total loss?
options: The KL term is always larger than reconstruction loss.
KL only matters for unconditional VAEs.
The total loss can't be computed without it.
A fine total can hide a KL near zero.
questions.explanation: Collapse shows up in the KL term, not necessarily in the sum.

questions.prompt: FID was 2.7411 for real against generated and 0.0856 for real against real. About how many times the baseline is that? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation: 2.7411 / 0.0856 = 32.0, far above the real-vs-real floor despite perfect class accuracy.

questions.prompt: Every generated sample was classified correctly, yet diversity was 0.442 against 1.920 for real data. What does that show?
options: The generator is ready to ship.
Real data is less varied than generated data.
Accuracy alone can't certify a generator.
The diversity metric is broken, since accuracy is perfect.
questions.explanation: The generator learned what makes a 3 a 3 without the full spread of real 3s. Procedure 75.4 checks both.

refLinks.label: §75.2.4 Classification Correctness and Distributional Realism Are Different Things

questions.prompt: Which changes does the chapter say a production version of this pipeline would need? Select all that apply.
options: A real-resolution backbone, not a 5,000-parameter toy
A pretrained diffusion model instead of a from-scratch VAE
A strong feature extractor such as Inception-v3 for FID
Removing the evaluation stage once accuracy hits 100%
questions.explanation: It also calls for a larger evaluation set for stable FID. The pipeline's shape carries over. Dropping evaluation contradicts the chapter's lesson.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain, in your own words, why the same three chapters' individual tutorials could not have caught the `BatchNorm` eval-mode bug this chapter found.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Each individual tutorial tests its component in isolation with its own controlled setup: the backbone's own tutorial trains and evaluates it directly (correctly in `.eval()` mode where needed for its own tests), and the VAE's tutorial doesn't reuse an external backbone at all. The `BatchNorm` bug only appears when the backbone is later reused as a frozen feature extractor *inside a different component's pipeline* without an explicit `.eval()` call: an integration-specific mistake no single chapter's isolated tutorial exercises.

bookExercises.prompt: State the symptom and the fix for posterior collapse, referencing Listing 75.3.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Symptom: KL loss collapses toward 0.0000 and generated samples ignore both the latent code `z` and the conditioning signal, producing generic outputs regardless of the requested class. Fix: lower `BETA` (this chapter used `BETA=0.5` too high, causing collapse, and fixed it by lowering to `BETA=0.1`).

bookExercises.prompt: Using this chapter's measured transfer-learning table, compute the absolute and relative improvement fine-tuning achieved over feature extraction, and explain why 16 total labelled examples was still enough for fine-tuning to win, referencing Chapter 69's guidance.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Absolute improvement: $0.9556 - 0.8790 = 0.0766$ (7.66 percentage points). Relative improvement: $0.0766 / 0.8790 \approx 8.7\%$. Sixteen total labelled examples (8-shot × 2 classes) was still enough for fine-tuning to win because, per Chapter 69's guidance, fine-tuning a backbone already pretrained on visually related classes (the other 8 digit classes) only needs to adapt already-relevant low/mid-level features to the two new classes, rather than learning useful features from scratch. The backbone's prior knowledge substitutes for a larger labelled set.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 75.4, trace through what decision the procedure would produce for a hypothetical generator that scored 1.0000 on class-conditional accuracy but had a FID-vs-baseline ratio of 50x (versus this chapter's measured 32x) and a diversity ratio of 0.1 (versus this chapter's measured ~0.23). Justify the decision using this chapter's own numbers as a reference point.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Per Listing 75.4's logic: perfect class-conditional accuracy (1.0000) alone is insufficient evidence of quality, since this chapter's own measured FID-vs-baseline ratio (2.8034/0.0856 ≈ 32.75x, "33x") and diversity ratio (0.356/1.920 ≈ 0.185, "~0.19") already indicate a real generated-vs-real quality gap despite perfect conditional accuracy. A hypothetical generator with an even worse 50x FID ratio and 0.1 diversity ratio would fail the decision procedure more severely. The perfect accuracy score would be recognized as necessary but not sufficient, since it only confirms the generator reliably encodes class identity, not that its outputs are diverse or realistic.

bookExercises.prompt: This chapter measured the held-out classes 8/9 embedding distance at 1.35, versus 2.6-7.6 for pretrained-class pairs. Using Listing 75.1, explain what practical effect this weaker separation would have on the generator's ability to produce a recognizably distinct digit for class 8 versus class 9.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A weaker embedding-space separation between classes 8 and 9 (1.35 vs. 2.6-7.6 for pretrained-class pairs) means the class-conditioning signal fed to the generator is less distinct between the two held-out classes. Practically, the generator has a harder time producing outputs for class 8 that are clearly visually distinguishable from class 9, since the conditioning vectors it's working from are themselves closer together than for well-separated pretrained classes, risking more visual confusability between the two generated digit classes specifically.

bookExercises.prompt: A customer's team has built a pipeline structurally identical to this chapter's (backbone, transfer learning, conditional generator, evaluation), and reports "our generator hits 100% conditional accuracy, so it's ready to ship." Using this chapter's Worked Example, write the two or three sentences you would say to them before agreeing.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "100% conditional accuracy only tells us the generator reliably produces outputs the backbone classifies as the requested class. It says nothing about whether those outputs are diverse or realistic. Before agreeing it's ready to ship, I'd want to see the FID-vs-real-baseline ratio and a diversity check, since this chapter's own pipeline hit perfect conditional accuracy while still showing a real quality gap on both those other measures."

bookExercises.prompt: Using this chapter's Trade-offs section, list the four specific changes needed to move this pipeline's *shape* from toy scale to production scale, and explain in one sentence why the shape itself does not need to change.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Four changes: (1) swap the toy backbone/VAE for production-scale architectures with far more parameters; (2) use real, larger labelled and unlabelled datasets instead of the digits dataset; (3) run training on real GPU infrastructure instead of toy-scale compute; (4) use the real Inception-v3 (or similar) feature extractor for FID/evaluation instead of the toy backbone. The pipeline *shape* itself (backbone → adapt → generate → evaluate) doesn't need to change because that dependency structure (classification signal informing generation, generation being evaluated by a feature extractor) is architecture-agnostic; only the scale of each piece changes.

bookExercises.prompt: Review your own solutions to this track's earlier exercises (Chapters 67-74). Identify one place where a shortcut or simplification you made would, if chained into a pipeline the way this chapter chains its three pieces, plausibly surface a bug analogous to the two found here.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only; depends on the specific earlier-chapter exercise answers given. The exercise asks for genuine self-review: a plausible category of answer is any earlier simplification (e.g. skipping an eval-mode call, assuming a hyperparameter that worked "in isolation" would transfer unchanged once chained into a larger pipeline) that this chapter's own two bugs (BatchNorm eval-mode, posterior collapse from an untested BETA) exemplify as a class of integration-only failure.
